title: Drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
hook: only Luke tells of the angel and the sweat like drops of blood

segments.voice: Yesterday, the apostles argued about greatness, and Jesus said he was among them as one who serves. Your line was as one that serveth. What job did you do unasked? Day four hundred eighty-one.

It's late. The supper is over. Jesus goes out, with his disciples following, to the Mount of Olives, to a place Luke says he went as he was accustomed. A familiar spot. Somewhere he'd prayed before. A chair by a window, a corner of a church, a walk taken when something is too heavy: some people keep a place like that. He tells the disciples to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he goes on a little further, about a stone's throw, and kneels down. Today, what happened when he did.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, AFTER SUPPER.` → `A PLACE HE WENT AS ACCUSTOMED.` → `A STONE'S THROW FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Kneeling, he prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." The chalice is the cup of suffering ahead. He asks honestly for it to pass, and then hands the decision over. And then Luke gives us two details no other Gospel has: "And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer. And his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground." Look at the order. The angel comes, and the agony doesn't stop. It deepens. He prays the longer. The angel doesn't take the cup away. The angel helps him drink it. In Luke's picture, strength from heaven isn't an exit. It's company in it. Agony, in Luke's Greek, is agonia, a word that could describe an athlete's strain before a contest, as well as deep anguish. And the sweat is like drops of blood: Luke says as, like. Readers have long debated whether he means real blood or a comparison for heavy, dark drops. The text doesn't settle it. Something else worth knowing: some early manuscripts of Luke don't have these two verses. The Church receives them as Scripture, and they're in the Latin Vulgate and the Douay. And the disciples? He comes back and finds them sleeping for sorrow. Luke is gentle with them: it was grief that knocked them out. Catholics pray this moment as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden, and some keep a holy hour, an hour of prayer, remembering that in Matthew and Mark, Jesus asks his friends to watch one hour with him.
screen: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE.` · `AN ANGEL, AND THE AGONY DEEPENS.` · `AGONIA: THE STRAIN BEFORE THE RACE.` · `SLEEPING FOR SORROW.` · then, large: `HIS SWEAT AS DROPS OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone in agony. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone going through something terrible right now: a frightening diagnosis, a court date, an addiction, a night in an emergency room, a grief with no bottom. Picture them at their own stone's throw, alone. You can't take the cup away. But you can keep watch. Stay with them in your mind for these two minutes, the way the disciples were asked to. If you pray, ask that they be strengthened, as he was. The bell holds the time.
Drops of blood. Luke's picture of Jesus' agony on the Mount of Olives, his sweat like drops of blood, an angel strengthening him to go on. Today's word.
Your line: an angel strengthened him. Today, be a small strengthening for one person in a hard hour: a message, a visit, a minute of real attention. Day four hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Agony in the Garden as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, and some keep a holy hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, especially on Holy Thursday night.

original.note: Greek: agony, the strain and struggle of a contest; Luke's word for Jesus in the garden.

trapdoor: what you thought: agony just means terrible pain.
what it means: in Luke, it's the struggle of someone straining toward a contest he's chosen to face, and he prays the longer through it.
what a scholar hears: Luke 22:43–44 is missing from some early manuscripts but is in the Vulgate; agonia appears only here in the New Testament.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer says 'most of us' (narrator speaking for the listener) and drops the uncited 'across a valley'; the narrator's own claim about 'what strength from God can look like' is now framed as Luke's picture; 'many keep a holy hour' softened twice.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 22:42 and 22:43–44.
Manuscript note: 22:43–44 are absent from some early witnesses (e.g., P75, Vaticanus) but present in many others and in the Vulgate; the Church receives them as canonical. Confirm phrasing.
Agonia occurs only here in the New Testament; confirm. Its sense here (athletic strain before a contest vs. anguish) is debated; the teach now gives both.
Holy hour now tied to Matthew 26:40 and Mark 14:37 ('watch one hour'), since Luke has no such line; confirm.
Whether the sweat was actual blood (some link it to hematidrosis) is left open as the text uses 'as'. Confirm.
